ctas.label: Find the right unit for my surgery

intro: Ice works for about 20 minutes. Then it melts, the wrap slips, and someone refills it — 4 to 6 times a day in the first week after surgery. Steady-Cold Recovery ends that cycle. A quiet motorised unit circulates chilled water through a pad shaped to your joint, holding the cold steady for hours on one fill. On Polar Care Wave, a pump adds measured, cycling compression to move swelling out. You follow your surgeon's sessions; the machine keeps the cold.

whatIs.title: Three things ice can't do
paragraphs: 1. Held cold. Chilled water keeps circulating, so the pad stays at a set temperature. Wave has two settings (about 7°C and 10°C). Kodiak runs 6–8 hours on one fill of ice and water.
2. Shaped pads. Knee, shoulder, ankle, hip and back pads wrap the whole joint, so the cold reaches every side — not one spot under a towel.
3. Measured compression (Wave). A quiet pump cycles pressure at one of two set levels, then releases, gently pushing swelling away from the surgical site.
All three run on your surgeon's session plan — typically 20–30 minutes, several times a day.

symptoms.title: When Steady-Cold earns its place
items: The first 2 weeks after orthopaedic surgery — knee, shoulder, hip, ankle, spine.
The first 48 hours after an acute injury — sprain, muscle strain, a rolled ankle.
After physiotherapy sessions — less next-day soreness, so you keep going to rehab.
Sports injuries with heavy swelling — ankle sprain, hamstring tear, knee bruising.
Flares of inflammatory arthritis — when your doctor advises it.

causes.title: Same idea as ice. Different result.
items: How long it stays cold. Ice pack: about 20 minutes. Steady-Cold: hours, at a set temperature.
Coverage. Ice pack: one spot. Steady-Cold: pad shaped to the whole joint.
Compression. Ice pack: static wrap, often slips. Steady-Cold: measured and cycling (Wave).
4–6 sessions a day. Ice pack: needs someone to refill and re-wrap. Steady-Cold: one fill, press start.
While it runs. Ice pack: hold it in place. Steady-Cold: read, eat or rest.
Proof. Studies on motorised cold-and-compression units show patients use less pain medication after surgery.

treatment.title: A typical Steady-Cold plan
treatment.lead: Your surgeon sets the exact plan. Most look like this:
steps: Days 1–7 — 20–30 minute sessions, 4–6 times a day. This is when it matters most.
Days 8–14 — About 3 sessions a day as swelling settles.
Weeks 3–4 — 1–2 sessions a day, mostly after physio.
After week 6 — Store the unit for future injuries or family use.

productsHeading.title: Kodiak or Wave?
productsHeading.lead: Steady-Cold = Polar Care Kodiak (cold only). Steady-Cold + Active Compression = Polar Care Wave. Not sure? Tell us your surgery and date — we'll tell you which fits, or whether ice is enough for you.

whenToSeeDoctor.title: When not to use cold therapy
whenToSeeDoctor.lead: Check with your doctor first, and skip or pause it if you have:
items: Open wounds or unhealed incisions — until your surgeon says the wound is sealed.
Raynaud's or strong cold sensitivity — cold can trigger spasms in blood vessels.
Reduced feeling in the area — diabetic neuropathy or nerve damage; you may not feel it getting too cold.
Suspected DVT — leg swelling, redness or calf pain. Get checked first.
whenToSeeDoctor.note: Always keep a thin barrier (dressing, towel or sleeve) between the pad and your skin. The pad should never touch bare skin. Stop at once if the skin turns white, blue or grey, you start shivering hard, or the pain gets worse during a session — and call your surgeon.

faq.question: How is Steady-Cold different from a cheaper cold compression machine?
faq.answer: Ask three questions of any unit: what temperature does the pad hold, how long does one fill last, and what pressure does it apply? Breg publishes all three for Polar Care. Compare on those, not on the photo.

faq.question: How long is each session?
faq.answer: Usually 20–30 minutes, 3–6 times a day in the first week. Your surgeon will set the exact plan.

faq.question: Can I sleep with it on?
faq.answer: Not routinely. Long, unbroken cold can harm skin. Use timed sessions unless your surgeon says otherwise.

faq.question: Is ice good enough?
faq.answer: For a single sprain at home, often yes. For surgery recovery, where you need cold several times a day for two weeks, Steady-Cold holds the temperature and coverage that ice can't.

faq.question: Does cold therapy slow healing?
faq.answer: Short, timed sessions help recovery by easing pain enough for earlier movement. Hours of non-stop cold may not — which is why sessions are timed.

faq.question: Does it help knee osteoarthritis?
faq.answer: Less so. OA pain is mostly from wear, not fresh swelling, and many patients prefer heat. Cold can help during a sudden swollen flare. For daily OA pain, an offloader brace has stronger evidence.

faq.question: How long will I need it?
faq.answer: Most patients use it heavily for 1–2 weeks, then less often up to week 6.
